t: The cervix, HPV and cervical cancer screening
sub: Why cervical cancer starts in the transformation zone, how HPV E6 and E7 drive it, and how screening catches it early.

pretest.q: Which HPV protein inactivates the retinoblastoma (Rb) protein?
pretest.why: E7 binds Rb and releases E2F transcription factors, so the cell passes from G1 into S phase without its normal checkpoint; E6 is the partner protein that destroys p53.

w.E6: E6 attacks the other brake: it binds p53 and tags it for ubiquitin-mediated destruction, so damaged cells avoid arrest and apoptosis.
w.L1: L1 is the major capsid protein that builds the viral shell; the vaccine uses it to make virus-like particles, and it has no role in the cell cycle.
w.E2: E2 is the viral repressor that normally keeps E6 and E7 low; integration into host DNA disrupts E2, which is why expression of the oncoproteins rises.

pretest.q: Where on the cervix does squamous metaplasia create the cells that high-risk HPV transforms?
pretest.why: Estrogen everts columnar epithelium onto the ectocervix, and acidic vaginal fluid drives it to become squamous. The immature metaplastic cells of this transformation zone are the ones HPV infects and transforms.

w.Internal os: The internal os is where the endocervical canal meets the uterine cavity; it is lined by glandular cells and is not the usual site of squamous neoplasia.
w.Mid-portion of the ectocervix: The outer ectocervix carries mature, glycogen-rich squamous epithelium that finished metaplasia long ago, so it is far less vulnerable to viral transformation.
w.Vaginal fornix: The fornix is lined by vaginal squamous epithelium; vaginal cancers are rare and usually spread from the cervix rather than arising there first.

pretest.q: A 22-year-old on a combined oral contraceptive has mucoid discharge and postcoital spotting; the cervix shows a red ring around the os and cytology is normal. What explains this?
pretest.why: Estrogen everts the columnar endocervical lining onto the ectocervix, where its thin, fragile cells secrete mucus and bleed on contact. Ectropion is benign and common with oral contraceptives, adolescence and pregnancy.

w.Invasive squamous cell carcinoma: Invasive cancer presents with a friable, exophytic or ulcerated mass and abnormal cytology or biopsy; a smooth red ring with a normal Pap points to benign ectropion.
w.Nabothian cyst: A nabothian cyst is a smooth, mucus-filled dome from a blocked crypt; it does not cause discharge or bleeding or appear as a red ring around the os.
w.Cervical stenosis: Stenosis narrows the os after excision, radiation or atrophy and traps menstrual blood, causing cyclic pain or hematometra rather than a red, bleeding ring.

body: Why does cervical cancer start in the transformation zone?

The cervix has two linings that meet at a line. The **ectocervix**, the part that bulges into the vagina, is covered by tough nonkeratinized stratified squamous epithelium, like the vagina. The endocervix lines the canal with mucus-secreting columnar cells that fold into branching crypts, the **plicae palmatae** or "palm folds", which act as the cervical glands. Estrogen at puberty everts the columnar lining onto the ectocervix, and the acidic vagina then converts that exposed lining to squamous epithelium by **metaplasia**. The band between the original and the active squamocolumnar junction is the {{rp13_tz|transformation zone}}, and its immature metaplastic cells are the cells that high-risk HPV infects and transforms.

Endocervical **mucus** changes with the cycle: estrogen near ovulation makes it abundant, thin, alkaline and stretchy so sperm can pass and survive, and progesterone thickens it into a barrier. When metaplastic epithelium grows over a crypt opening, the trapped mucus forms a {{rp13_nabothian|nabothian cyst}}, a smooth, harmless dome that needs no treatment. Sampling also depends on the zone. A Pap specimen with too few squamous cells, or one hidden by blood or inflammation, is reported as **unsatisfactory** and repeated in 2 to 4 months. A satisfactory specimen can still lack an **endocervical component**: no endocervical or metaplastic cells were seen, the report says so, and a negative result is then a possible false-negative.
After menopause the junction hides in the canal

Low estrogen lets the squamocolumnar junction recede up the endocervical canal, so a spatula on the ectocervix can miss the **transformation zone**. Use an endocervical brush, and expect colposcopy to be inadequate when the whole junction cannot be seen; **endocervical curettage** then samples the canal. A hidden zone is why a normal Pap in an older woman can be a false-negative.
How can an altered cervix change what it does?

Eversion is normal in young women, but a large area of exposed columnar epithelium, a red, velvety ring around the os, is called {{rp13_ectropion|ectropion}}. It is common in adolescence, in pregnancy and with combined oral contraceptives, because estrogen drives eversion. The fragile columnar layer gives a mucoid discharge and bleeding after intercourse. Ectropion is benign and needs treatment only if the symptoms bother her, but contact bleeding still calls for a Pap test to exclude cervicitis and cancer.

Scarring changes the canal in the opposite direction. **Stenosis** of the os follows excision of the zone, radiation or severe inflammation, and low estrogen can narrow it after menopause. When the os closes, menstrual blood cannot escape and the uterus fills with blood, **hematometra**, causing cyclic pain and an enlarged uterus in a patient who is not bleeding. A shortened, weakened cervix after excision can instead dilate painlessly in pregnancy: **cervical insufficiency**. Advanced cancer compresses the ureters through the parametria and causes hydronephrosis.
How does high-risk HPV turn a cervical cell into a cancer cell?

Human papillomavirus is a small, nonenveloped DNA virus that reaches cells of the basal layer through tiny epithelial breaks. Low-risk types 6 and 11 cause genital warts, while **high-risk** types, above all 16 and then 18, cause most cervical cancers. Most infections clear within one to two years, so the requirement for cancer is **persistent** infection. Persistence lets the viral genome **integrate** into host DNA, and integration usually breaks the viral E2 gene, the repressor that keeps the E6 and E7 oncogenes quiet. With E2 gone, E6 and E7 are overexpressed and switch off two key tumor suppressors.
Arrest and apoptosis after DNA damage
The G1 checkpoint, as E2F is released
Cells enter S phase at will; p16 rises
Explains why integration is the key step
E6 destroys p53; E7 disables Rb

**E6** binds p53 and sends it to the proteasome, and **E7** binds Rb and frees E2F. Because working Rb normally holds p16 down, E7 activity makes p16 pile up, so diffuse block {{rp13_p16|p16 staining}} marks a lesion driven by high-risk HPV.
How do CIN grades map onto LSIL and HSIL?

**Cervical intraepithelial neoplasia** (CIN) is graded by how far atypical cells, which begin in the basal layer, climb up the epithelium. In CIN 1 they occupy the **lower third**, in CIN 2 the lower two-thirds, and in CIN 3 more than two-thirds up to the full thickness, which includes **carcinoma in situ**. Because the basement membrane is intact in every grade, CIN cannot metastasize. The two-tier squamous intraepithelial lesion terms group CIN 1 as LSIL and CIN 2 or 3 as HSIL. {{rp13_koil|Koilocytes}}, squamous cells with enlarged, hyperchromatic, wrinkled (raisinoid) nuclei and a clear perinuclear halo, show productive viral infection and are typical of LSIL. CIN 1 usually regresses, whereas CIN 3 tends to progress, and diffuse p16 staining settles a lesion that looks like CIN 2 as HSIL.

Cytology is reported with the {{rp13_bethesda|Bethesda System}}, which states whether the specimen is satisfactory and has an endocervical component, then names the finding: negative for intraepithelial lesion or malignancy (NILM); atypical squamous cells of undetermined significance (ASC-US), the commonest abnormal result; ASC-H, which cannot exclude HSIL; LSIL; HSIL; and atypical glandular cells (AGC), which point to the endocervix or endometrium. Cytology and biopsy match only roughly, so results are acted on by risk, not by label.
From HPV infection to invasive carcinoma
Virus enters immature basal cells through microabrasions, and most women clear it within two years.
In a minority the infection persists, especially with type 16, smoking or immunosuppression, and the viral DNA integrates into the host genome.
Loss of E2 releases the oncoproteins, p53 and Rb stop working, and dividing cells collect mutations; this is CIN 2 and CIN 3.
Invasion of the stroma turns HSIL into carcinoma, usually over many years, so screening every few years works.
Who is screened, with which test, and how often?

Screening looks for **precancer** in people without symptoms, and its rules follow how slowly HPV lesions progress. It is done during a speculum exam: a spatula and an endocervical brush sample the ectocervix, the transformation zone and the canal into liquid preservative, which can be tested by cytology or for HPV. Average-risk screening starts at age 21, whatever the sexual history. The USPSTF (2018) recommends **cytology** alone every 3 years from 21 to 29, because HPV infection is common and transient at these ages and testing for it would flag many lesions destined to regress. From 30 to 65 it accepts primary HPV testing every 5 years, a **cotest** (cytology plus HPV) every 5 years, or cytology every 3 years.

The American Cancer Society (ACS, 2020) starts later and leans on HPV: primary HPV testing every 5 years from 25 to 65. Both stop after 65 with adequately negative results, and after total hysterectomy for benign disease. A family history of cervical cancer does not change these schedules, because HPV and age drive the risk, unlike breast, ovarian and colon screening, which start earlier with a first-degree relative or a BRCA or Lynch mutation. These are the guidelines as of 2025.
Primary HPV every 5 years, cotest every 5, or cytology every 3
Primary HPV every 5 years (cotest or cytology if HPV is unavailable)
Stop with no CIN 2 or worse in 25 years
Separate guideline: start within a year of sexual debut, screen more often, for life
What happens after an abnormal screening result?

Screening, diagnosis and treatment are separate steps. HPV vaccination is primary prevention, because it stops infection; screening is **secondary prevention**, because it finds precancer early enough to remove. A screening test sorts well people by risk and never makes a diagnosis. **Diagnosis** comes from {{rp13_colpo|colposcopy}}: the cervix is magnified after acetic acid, abnormal areas turn white and are biopsied, with endocervical curettage when the zone extends up the canal. ASCCP guidelines (2019) base each decision on the estimated risk of CIN 3 or worse, which combines today's result with past results (the ASCCP app does the calculation); at roughly 4 percent immediate risk, colposcopy is advised.
Return at the routine interval for age and HPV result
**Reflex** HPV test on the same sample: positive goes to colposcopy, negative returns to repeat testing in 3 years
Colposcopy usually; repeat testing in a year if a recent HPV test was negative
High-grade lesion cannot be excluded, or is present
Colposcopy with biopsy; immediate excision is allowed when the risk of CIN 3 is very high
Colposcopy with endocervical curettage, plus **endometrial biopsy** from age 35 or with risk factors

Biopsy-proven CIN 1 is usually watched with repeat testing, because most regress. HSIL (CIN 2 or 3) is excised with a {{rp13_leep|loop electrosurgical excision procedure}} (LEEP), a thin electrified wire loop used in the office under local anesthesia, or by **cold-knife** conization, a scalpel cone cut in the operating room that leaves undamaged margins and is preferred when glandular disease is suspected. Both give a specimen. **Ablation** with cryotherapy or laser gives none, so it is reserved for CIN 2 or 3 when the whole lesion is visible, the canal is clear and invasion has been excluded. Hysterectomy is not first-line.
Excision treats precancer but can weaken the cervix

Removing a cone of cervical stroma treats HSIL, but the shorter, weaker cervix can dilate painlessly in a later pregnancy: **cervical insufficiency**, with second-trimester loss or **preterm** birth. Cold-knife cones remove more tissue and carry more risk than LEEP, and punch biopsies carry essentially none.
Why does dysplastic epithelium turn white when acetic acid is applied at colposcopy?

Acetic acid briefly dehydrates cells and coagulates their nuclear proteins. Normal mature squamous cells are mostly cytoplasm and glycogen, so light passes through them to the red stroma beneath and the surface looks pink. Dysplastic cells have large nuclei and little cytoplasm, so a field of them is dense with coagulated nuclear protein that reflects light, and the area turns acetowhite. Because the whitening tracks nuclear density, it marks where the highest-grade cells are, which is exactly where the colposcopist aims the biopsy.
How does invasive cervical cancer present, and how does it kill?

About three-quarters of invasive cervical cancers are **squamous cell carcinoma**; adenocarcinoma, from the glandular cells of the canal, comes second and is linked more closely to HPV 18. Risk follows HPV exposure and persistence: early first intercourse, many partners, smoking, immunosuppression, HIV and long gaps in screening. Early cancers are silent and found only by screening, while larger tumors cause **postcoital** bleeding, irregular bleeding and a watery, blood-tinged discharge. The tumor spreads by direct extension into the parametria and pelvic side walls, where it compresses the ureters, and the resulting bilateral **hydronephrosis** and renal failure are a leading cause of death. Stage guides treatment: early disease confined to the cervix is cured by surgery, and tumor beyond it needs chemoradiation.
How do vaccination, HIV and cervicitis change the plan?

The HPV **vaccine** is primary prevention. The **9-valent** vaccine contains recombinant L1 capsid proteins that self-assemble into virus-like particles, so it carries no viral DNA and cannot cause infection; it covers types 6, 11, 16, 18, 31, 33, 45, 52 and 58. It is given routinely at age 11 or 12, as two doses if started before 15 and three doses after that or with immunosuppression, with catch-up through age 26 and shared decisions from 27 to 45. Vaccinated women still follow the same screening schedule, because the vaccine does not cover every oncogenic type or clear an infection already present.

HIV changes the timeline because immunosuppression lets HPV persist: the lower the **CD4** count, the weaker the clearance of infection and the higher the rates of persistent HPV, CIN and cancer. Women with HIV begin screening within a year of sexual debut or at diagnosis, have annual cytology until three consecutive results are normal and then every 3 years, and never age out at 65. People with HIV also face more **anal cancer**, because the anal canal has its own transformation zone that the same virus infects, so they are offered anal cytology, and an abnormal result leads to high-resolution **anoscopy** with biopsy.

**Cervicitis** is a separate problem: chlamydia or gonorrhea causes a mucopurulent endocervical discharge and a friable cervix that bleeds when swabbed, and nucleic acid amplification testing finds the organism. Both the patient and her partner are treated, because the infection can ascend to cause pelvic inflammatory disease.
Age 24 and younger, or older with risk
At least once, and in pregnancy

body.q: A 60-year-old's colposcopy cannot show the whole squamocolumnar junction. Which reasoning best explains the next step?
o: Low estrogen has drawn the junction up the canal, so the unseen zone must be sampled by endocervical curettage
The junction has spread outward across the ectocervix after menopause, so a wider ectocervical biopsy will capture the zone
Low estrogen has made the transformation zone disappear, so the patient no longer needs any cervical sampling
Chronic inflammation has hidden the junction, so treating cervicitis first will bring the zone back into view
body.why: Estrogen keeps the cervix large and everted; after menopause the cervix shrinks and the squamocolumnar junction retreats into the endocervical canal. The transformation zone still exists, and it is still where HPV-driven lesions live, but it is now out of sight, so the colposcopy is inadequate. Endocervical curettage samples the canal where the hidden zone lies. Biopsying the visible ectocervix samples mature squamous epithelium that is rarely the problem, and inflammation does not set the junction's position.

body: Why can HPV testing be spaced every 5 years when cytology alone needs every 3 years?

A negative HPV test means no high-risk virus is present, and without the virus a precancer cannot develop, so the risk of CIN 3 over the next five years is very low. Cytology is a single look at cells and misses a meaningful share of existing lesions, so its negative result is less reassuring and must be repeated sooner. Because progression from new infection to invasive cancer usually takes many years, a five-year gap after a negative HPV test still catches lesions long before they invade.

grid.q: Which of these raise the risk of cervical cancer?
items: HIV infection with a low CD4 count
